Chapter 19

The grid: a thousand cells out of a million

Only the cells the scroll position reveals exist in the DOM, positioned absolutely inside a canvas the size of the whole sheet. Two numbers change on scroll, and the two numbers change which cells are rendered. One cell snippet, four layers.

By the end of this chapter

Build a two-axis virtualised grid with frozen panes as sticky layers, and know exactly what is reactive in it and what is not.

Three ideas in the header. Only visible cells exist. Cell values are not reactive — one signal, sheet.version, redraws the viewport. And every decoration — selection, formula-reference colours, other people’s cursors, the “changed by somebody else” flash — is a class on a cell, not an overlay, because an overlay would need its own copy of the geometry and would come apart at the frozen panes.

Geometry

The axes are $derived from the sheet’s SvelteMaps — iterating a SvelteMap is tracked, so a resize rebuilds them. The row and column counts grow with the content, with the scroll position, and with the active cell, so a sheet is always a little bigger than what is in it and never smaller than what has been reached. rows and cols are the indexes the scroll reveals, with two rows of overscan so a fast scroll does not show a blank band.

Why scroll position is state and not read from the element

Every visible cell’s position depends on where the viewport is scrolled. If the grid read element.scrollTop inside the template, nothing would re-run when it changed. Two $state numbers written by an onscroll handler are what let a scroll be a reactive event: the numbers change, rows and cols re-derive, and the each blocks add and remove cells. bind:scrollTop does not exist on elements — the first version tried it — so the handler is the honest way.

One snippet, four layers

A snippet with parameters is a template function. cell(r, c, top, left) renders one cell at a position, and its eight declaration tags — {const value = $derived(sheet.value(r, c))} and the seven beside it — compute everything the cell shows from the sheet and the decorations. Declaration tags arrived in Svelte 5.56 and made {@const} legacy. The $derived keeps the reactivity {@const} had: when the sheet changes, value is worked out again. A bare {const value = sheet.value(r, c)} would be worked out once, like a const in the script, and the cell’s number, true/false and error styling would stop following its value; its text would still update, because {sheet.display(r, c)} is read straight in the markup. A declaration tag is visible to its siblings and their children in the same lexical scope, so these eight, the first children of the snippet, reach the cell’s markup and nothing outside the snippet. The header awaits the same way, {const me = $derived(await whoAmI())} (ch. 30). The class array is the whole visual state: numeric alignment, selection edges, formula highlight edges, the flash, the fill target. The editor mounts inside the cell being edited, so it is positioned by the same geometry as everything else.

When a declaration tag needs $derived, and when it does not

A declaration tag runs when its block is made, like a const at the top of a function. That is all {const spec = FUNCTIONS.get(name)} needs in the formula bar’s suggestion list: the each is keyed by name, so an item’s name never changes while the item exists, the table of functions never changes at all, and the answer worked out once is the answer for good. The same is true of the lesson’s cell names, of the .for(id) form each workspace card gets, and of the session the cell editor holds. {const value = $derived(sheet.value(r, c))} is the other case. The snippet’s block lives while the cell is on screen, and what the cell holds changes underneath it, so the value must be worked out again whenever what it read changes — which is what $derived adds, at the price of one signal per cell. Ask one question: can anything this expression reads change while the block is alive? If not, write the plain tag; a $derived around a value nothing can change is a signal with nothing to signal. The await tags are always $derived, because the query they await is refreshed in place.

Frozen panes are the same snippet rendered in extra layers: frozen rows at the top, frozen columns at the left, and the corner where they meet, each with a different origin. The layers are sticky, and the trick that makes that work is in the stylesheet.

Each sticky layer is zero-sized: it takes no space in the canvas’s flow, and its absolutely positioned children overflow visibly and move with the canvas on the other axis. That is how the column headers stay at the top while scrolling down and still scroll sideways — with no JavaScript synchronising two scrollers, which is the way every grid used to do it and the way every grid got out of step.

The two effects

Both are real side effects, which is what $effect is for. The first clears the flash set after a timer and cancels the timer if the set changes first. The second keeps the active cell on screen by writing to the element’s scrollTop — untrack around the reads so that the effect depends only on sheet.anchor, not on the scroll position it is about to change, which would otherwise loop.

Three elements nest here, and the comment says what each is for: the grid takes the keys, the viewport scrolls, and the canvas is the size of the whole sheet, which is what gives the viewport something to scroll. The block stops where the canvas opens; inside it come the snippet, the header layers, and the four layers it renders into from earlier in the chapter. The outer element is role="grid" with aria-rowcount, aria-colcount, aria-multiselectable and aria-activedescendant pointing at the active cell’s id — the ARIA grid pattern, which is how a screen reader knows this is a spreadsheet and where in it the person is.

After the canvas, as the last child of the grid, a polite live region announces the active cell’s address, value and formula on every move. announcement is a $derived that reads sheet.version as well as the anchor, so a recalculation that changes the active cell’s value is announced too, and visually-hidden keeps the text off the screen but in the accessibility tree.

Checkpoint

  • You can say which four things are $state in the grid and why cell values are not.
  • You can explain how a sticky zero-sized layer keeps column headers at the top while scrolling sideways.
  • You can say why the scroll-into-view effect wraps its reads in untrack.
